name: Darce Choke from Darce Control
description: Master the Darce Choke finish from Darce Control position. Learn grip mechanics, hip positioning, shoulder pressure, and finishing details for this high-percentage blood choke.
summary: The Darce Choke from Darce Control is an arm-in blood choke finished by locking a figure-four grip, dropping the hip to the mat, and extending the body to compress both carotid arteries against the opponent's trapped shoulder.
overview:
The Darce Choke from Darce Control represents the finishing phase of one of the most effective arm-triangle variations in modern grappling. Unlike entries from scrambles or turtle where the attacker must simultaneously establish control and threaten the choke, executing from an already-secured Darce Control position allows the attacker to focus entirely on grip refinement, hip placement, and progressive compression. The position-specific advantage lies in having the opponent's posture already broken and arm already trapped, eliminating two of the three major defensive windows.

The finishing mechanics hinge on three coordinated actions: deepening the choking arm so the blade of the forearm sits directly across the carotid arteries, dropping the hip to the mat on the choking side to create a structural wedge, and driving shoulder pressure forward to close the remaining space around the neck. The figure-four grip transforms the arms into a self-tightening noose where any defensive movement by the opponent actually increases compression. Timing the hip drop with the grip lock is the critical skill that separates reliable finishers from those who stall in the control position.

From a strategic standpoint, the Darce finish from established control carries a high completion rate because the opponent's defensive options are already limited. The primary defensive window occurs before the hip drop—once the attacker commits their weight to the mat and extends through the choking structure, the submission becomes extremely difficult to escape. This makes recognizing and executing the transition from control to finish one of the most important skills in the front headlock attack chain.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to unconsciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate if released; prolonged compression can cause stroke

injury_risks.injury: Neck muscle strain from improper resistance
Shoulder impingement from trapped arm position

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum to allow tap recognition
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on partner's body
Any distress signal or loss of resistance
release_protocol: Immediately unclasp hands and release figure-four grip
Remove shoulder pressure from neck first
Extract choking arm slowly to avoid neck jerk
Allow partner to recover in seated or supine position
Monitor for 30+ seconds for dizziness or disorientation
If unconsciousness occurred, keep airway clear and seek medical evaluation
training_restrictions: Never apply full pressure in drilling—use positional control only
Never use competition speed or intensity in training
Always allow clear tap access with free hand
Never spike or jerk the choke—apply smooth progressive pressure
Stop immediately at any tap signal without waiting for confirmation
Never train this technique while fatigued or with impaired judgment

variations_and_setups.description: Drop the hip on the choking side to the mat and extend your body perpendicular to opponent's spine. The body extension creates structural leverage that closes the choke without requiring excessive arm strength. Most reliable finishing method from established Darce Control.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have a deep grip and opponent is flattened or on their side with limited mobility

variations_and_setups.description: Maintain the Darce grip while walking your hips around toward opponent's head in a quarter-circle arc. Each step tightens the choke incrementally by changing the compression angle. Finish by sprawling once hips reach the optimal perpendicular angle.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent is in turtle and you cannot immediately drop your hip due to their base preventing you from getting to the correct side

variations_and_setups.description: Instead of the traditional figure-four (RNC-style) grip, lock a palm-to-palm gable grip behind opponent's far shoulder. Provides stronger initial squeezing power and is faster to secure, though it offers less of a ratcheting effect than the figure-four.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent is actively defending the figure-four lock or when your arms are fatigued and you need maximum grip strength for a quick finish

attacker.name: from Darce Control Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to finish the Darce Choke from established Darce Control. Step-by-step finishing mechanics, grip details, hip positioning, and counters to common defensive responses.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Darce Choke from Darce Control means you have already won the positional battle—your arm is threaded, the grip is locked, and your opponent's posture is broken. The finishing phase requires converting that control into a completed strangle by refining three elements: grip depth across the carotid arteries, hip placement to create a structural wedge, and progressive shoulder pressure that closes any remaining space. The key insight is that finishing from established control is about precision and body mechanics rather than strength. Your body positioning does the choking work while your arms maintain the structure. Every adjustment should make the choke tighter without requiring more muscular effort, creating a self-reinforcing compression cycle that the defender cannot outlast.
key_principles: Depth before pressure: ensure the choking forearm blade sits directly across the carotid arteries before committing to the squeeze
Hip drop creates the wedge: dropping your hip to the mat on the choking side converts your entire body into a lever that closes the choke structurally
Shoulder drives perpendicular to spine: pressure vector should push opponent's head toward the mat, not along their spine
Elbows stay pinched: any gap between your elbows allows the opponent to create space for arm extraction or head escape
Extension finishes the choke: after the hip drop, straighten your body to elongate the choking structure and maximize carotid compression
Continuous micro-adjustments: small positional changes in response to defensive movement keep tightening the choke rather than maintaining static pressure
setup_requirements: Darce grip established with choking arm threaded under opponent's near armpit and hand reaching past the far side of their neck
Figure-four or gable grip locked with elbows pinched together eliminating defensive space
Opponent's posture broken with head below hips and unable to create effective frames
Chest-to-back connection maintained with shoulder pressure driving into the side of opponent's head
Control of opponent's trapped arm confirmed—it cannot be extracted without deliberate defensive effort

execution_steps.description: Confirm your choking arm's forearm blade sits directly across the carotid arteries on the near side of opponent's neck. Your hand should reach past the far side of their neck toward their far shoulder. If shallow, re-swim the arm deeper before committing to the finish.

Secure your free hand on your own bicep (RNC-style figure-four) or lock a palm-to-palm gable grip. Pinch your elbows together tightly to eliminate any gaps. The grip lock transforms your arms into a closed loop around opponent's neck and trapped arm.

Step your hips toward the side of your choking arm so your body is perpendicular to opponent's spine. Each step incrementally changes the compression angle and tightens the choke. Maintain chest contact throughout the hip walk to prevent opponent from creating escape space.

Lower your hip on the choking side to the mat beside opponent's body. This hip drop is the critical mechanical action that converts arm pressure into full-body structural compression. Your body weight now drives the choke rather than muscular effort from your arms alone.

Push your shoulder into the side of opponent's head with the pressure vector aimed perpendicular to their spine and toward the mat. Keep your head low next to theirs. This shoulder wedge closes the final gap on the far-side carotid artery, completing the bilateral compression needed for the blood choke.

Straighten your body by extending your legs away from opponent while maintaining the grip and shoulder pressure. This extension elongates the choking structure, tightening the loop around the neck without requiring additional arm strength. Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds to allow tap recognition.

Watch for tap signals including hand tap, foot tap, verbal tap, or body going limp. Release immediately upon any signal by unclamping hands and removing shoulder pressure first. If opponent does not tap within 8-10 seconds of full extension with correct mechanics, reassess grip depth and angle before re-applying.

common_counters.counter: Arm extraction—opponent uses free hand to pull trapped arm out of the choke structure
common_counters.your_response: Pinch elbows tighter and drive shoulder pressure deeper the moment you feel the trapped arm moving. If extraction begins, immediately increase chest-to-back connection and consider transitioning to anaconda grip or standard arm triangle before the arm fully clears.

common_counters.counter: Rolling through—opponent barrel rolls toward the choking arm side to relieve pressure and scramble
common_counters.your_response: Follow the roll and maintain the grip. A roll toward the choking side often tightens the choke if you stay connected. If they complete the roll to guard, be prepared to finish from inside their guard or transition to mount by posting and stepping over.

common_counters.counter: Turning into the choke—opponent rotates to face you, attempting to square up and establish inside position
common_counters.your_response: Sprawl your hips back and drive shoulder pressure down to prevent the turn from completing. If they get partially turned, transition to mount or back control rather than fighting to maintain the darce angle. The turn itself often exposes the back.

common_counters.counter: Posturing up—opponent drives upward to create space and reduce compression
common_counters.your_response: Use their upward movement to deepen your grip by pulling your choking arm further through. Their posture attempt opens space for your arm to travel deeper. As they rise, snap them back down with the grip and immediately commit to the hip drop finish while they are momentarily off-balance.

common_errors.error: Shallow grip—choking forearm sits on the shoulder or jaw instead of across the carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Choke becomes a crank or pressure hold rather than a blood choke, allowing opponent to endure indefinitely while working systematic escape
common_errors.correction: Before committing to the finish, verify the blade of your forearm contacts the side of the neck directly over the carotid. Re-swim the arm deeper if needed—sacrificing 2 seconds for grip depth is always worth it.

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arms instead of using body mechanics to close the choke
common_errors.consequence: Forearms fatigue within 15-20 seconds, grip loosens, and opponent escapes as your strength fades
common_errors.correction: Use the hip drop and body extension to create structural compression. Your arms maintain the loop shape while your body weight and position do the squeezing work.

common_errors.error: Hip positioned on the wrong side or directly behind opponent instead of perpendicular
common_errors.consequence: No structural wedge is created, forcing arm-only compression which is insufficient against a tucked chin and strong neck
common_errors.correction: Walk your hips to the choking-arm side until your body is roughly perpendicular to opponent's spine. The hip drop must land beside their body, not behind it.

common_errors.error: Lifting head up and away from opponent during the finish
common_errors.consequence: Creates space under the armpit that allows arm extraction and relieves shoulder pressure on the neck
common_errors.correction: Keep your head down and tight next to opponent's head throughout the entire finish. Think about driving your ear toward the mat on the far side of their head.

common_errors.error: Rushing the finish without securing proper angle and depth
common_errors.consequence: Opponent survives the initial squeeze attempt and uses the recovery window to execute escape sequences
common_errors.correction: Treat the finish as a multi-step process: verify depth, lock grip, walk hips, drop hip, drive shoulder, extend. Each step makes the next more effective.

common_errors.error: Elbows flaring out during the squeeze, creating gaps in the choke structure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can wedge fingers or forearm into the gap and create enough space to extract the trapped arm or relieve carotid pressure
common_errors.correction: Actively pinch elbows together throughout the finish. Think about touching your elbows to each other—even if anatomically impossible, the intent keeps the structure tight.

training_progressions.focus: Developing correct arm depth and grip lock from static Darce Control
training_progressions.description: Partner holds turtle or side position with no resistance. Practice threading the choking arm to correct depth, locking the figure-four, and identifying the forearm-to-carotid contact point. Repeat 20 reps per side, partner providing feedback on pressure location.

training_progressions.focus: Drilling the hip walk, hip drop, and body extension as a connected chain
training_progressions.description: From locked Darce Control, practice the complete finishing sequence at 30% pressure. Focus on the hip walk angle, the timing of the hip drop, and extending the body to close the choke. Partner taps early to reinforce correct mechanics without risk.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining the finish against progressive resistance and common escapes
training_progressions.description: Partner offers 50-75% resistance using the primary counters: arm extraction, rolling through, and turning in. Attacker adjusts in real time—deepening grip, following rolls, or transitioning to alternatives. 3-minute rounds, reset after each finish or escape.

training_progressions.focus: Finishing under competition conditions from various entry points
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring starting from front headlock or turtle. Attacker must establish Darce Control and finish within 60 seconds against full resistance. Track completion rate and identify which defensive reactions cause the most difficulty. Increase to open rolling once completion rate exceeds 40%.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Darce Choke primarily target and how does the arm-in configuration create compression?
flashcards.answer: The Darce Choke targets both carotid arteries simultaneously through bilateral compression. The choking arm's forearm blade presses against the near-side carotid, while opponent's own trapped shoulder is driven into the far-side carotid by the figure-four grip and shoulder pressure. The arm-in configuration is essential because the opponent's trapped arm acts as a spacer that wedges their shoulder into the far-side artery—without the trapped arm, the choke loses half its compression mechanism.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins pulling their trapped arm free while you are setting up the finish—what adjustment prevents the escape?
flashcards.answer: Immediately pinch your elbows tighter together and increase chest-to-back connection to eliminate the space needed for extraction. Drive your shoulder pressure deeper into the side of their head to flatten them and reduce their mechanical ability to pull. If the arm is partially extracted, quickly transition to an anaconda grip by re-threading your arm over instead of under, or switch to a standard arm triangle if you can capture their arm on the other side of their neck.

flashcards.question: Why is the hip drop the critical mechanical action in the Darce finish, and what happens if you skip it?
flashcards.answer: The hip drop converts the choke from an arm-strength squeeze into a structural compression using your entire body weight. When your hip contacts the mat on the choking side, your body becomes a wedge that drives the choking structure closed through gravitational force and skeletal alignment rather than muscular effort. Without the hip drop, you rely solely on arm strength, which fatigues within 15-20 seconds and produces insufficient pressure against opponents with strong necks and good chin-tuck defense.

flashcards.question: What are the key safety considerations when applying the Darce Choke, and how fast does unconsciousness occur?
flashcards.answer: The Darce Choke compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously, which can cause unconsciousness in as little as 4-6 seconds once the choke is fully locked. Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds to allow tap recognition. Never jerk or spike the choke. Watch for all tap signals including verbal, hand tap, foot tap, and body going limp. Release immediately upon any signal by unclamping hands first, then removing shoulder pressure. If a training partner loses consciousness, place them in recovery position and monitor breathing.

trap: Jerk it tight to finish fast

flashcards.question: How should you release the Darce Choke after your training partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Release by first unclamping your hands to break the figure-four grip structure, then removing shoulder pressure from the neck. Extract your choking arm slowly—do not yank it out, as sudden removal can jerk the cervical spine. Allow your partner to recover in a seated or supine position. Monitor them for 30 seconds for signs of dizziness, disorientation, or delayed effects. If unconsciousness occurred at any point, keep their airway clear and seek medical evaluation even if they appear to recover quickly.
flashcards.answer_line: Unclamp grip, ease arm out slowly

plausible: Peel shoulder off before the hands
Sit them up, skip the 30s watch
trap: Yank the choking arm straight out

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks their chin hard and the choke stalls—what adjustments can you make to complete the finish?
flashcards.answer: A committed chin tuck blocks forearm penetration to the carotid arteries. First, verify your grip depth—if shallow, re-swim the arm deeper before re-attempting. If depth is correct, increase shoulder pressure perpendicular to their spine to force the head to turn, which opens the neck. Walk your hips further around toward their head to change the compression angle. If the chin tuck holds, transition to positional advancement (mount or north-south) rather than forcing a stalled choke, then re-attack from the improved position.

plausible: Wait for them to tire out
trap: Crank the neck to break tuck

flashcards.question: What is the point of no escape for the defender, and how do you recognize when the finish is secured?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the hip drop is complete, elbows are pinched, and body extension begins. At this stage, the structural compression is self-reinforcing—any defensive movement by the opponent tightens the choke further. You recognize the secured finish by feeling opponent's body relax slightly as their defensive frames collapse, their breathing becomes labored or stops, and their attempts to extract the trapped arm weaken noticeably. The choke is mechanically locked when you can feel both carotid pulses diminishing through your forearm contact.

plausible: Your chest is off their back

flashcards.question: In competition, your opponent is defending the Darce aggressively and the referee is watching for stalling—what is your finishing strategy?
flashcards.answer: In competition, commit to a decisive 15-second finishing window. Start by verifying grip depth, then execute the hip walk and hip drop as one explosive sequence rather than incrementally. If the choke is not producing defensive panic within 8 seconds of the hip drop, immediately transition to mount (step over) or back control (follow their escape direction) to score points and create new submission opportunities. Stalling in a stalled Darce burns clock and energy with no return. The threat of positional advancement often breaks the defensive shell more effectively than prolonged squeezing.

defender.name: from Darce Control Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend and escape the Darce Choke from Darce Control. Recognition cues, escape timing windows, arm extraction methods, and recovery paths for survival.
defender.overview: Defending the Darce Choke from established Darce Control is one of the most urgent defensive situations in grappling. Your opponent has already secured the grip, broken your posture, and trapped your arm—the finishing sequence can produce unconsciousness in seconds once committed. Successful defense requires immediate recognition that the finish is being initiated (hip walk, grip tightening, angle change) and decisive action during the narrow window before the hip drop locks the choke structurally. The defender must resist the instinct to pull away from the choke, which paradoxically tightens it, and instead move toward the attacker while working to extract the trapped arm or disrupt the finishing angle. Every second of hesitation allows the attacker to refine their position, so defensive responses must be trained to the level of automatic reaction.
key_principles: Act immediately—every second of delay allows the attacker to deepen the grip and improve their angle, shrinking your escape window exponentially
Move toward the choke, not away: turning into the attacker reduces the compression angle and creates space for arm extraction
Free the trapped arm first—the arm-in configuration is what makes the Darce effective, and removing it collapses the choke mechanics
Tuck the chin tight to the chest to prevent the forearm blade from settling directly on the carotid arteries
Maintain base and frames to prevent being flattened, which eliminates all escape leverage
Recognize the point of no return: if the hip drop is complete and body extension begins, tap immediately rather than risking unconsciousness
recognition_cues: Opponent begins walking their hips toward the choking-arm side, changing from a parallel position to a perpendicular angle relative to your spine
Grip tightens noticeably as opponent pinches elbows together and adjusts the figure-four or gable grip—you feel increased compression around your neck and shoulder
Shoulder pressure intensifies as opponent drives their weight forward and downward into the side of your head, pushing your face toward the mat
Opponent's hip begins dropping toward the mat on the choking side, signaling commitment to the finishing sequence

defensive_options.action: Arm extraction—use your free hand to grip your trapped arm and pull it toward your body while turning into opponent
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the grip tighten and before the hip drop. This is your highest-percentage escape and must be your first response.
defensive_options.if_successful: Choke structure collapses without the trapped arm; recover to turtle or establish guard
defensive_options.risk: If you commit both hands to extraction, you lose your framing ability and may be flattened

defensive_options.action: Step over escape—step your far leg over opponent's head and roll through to create a scramble
defensive_options.when_to_use: When opponent commits to the hip walk and their head is low, creating space for your leg to clear. Effective when arm extraction has been blocked.
defensive_options.if_successful: Scramble position where you can recover to guard or potentially reverse to top position
defensive_options.risk: Mistiming the step-over can expose your back and tighten the choke if opponent follows the roll

defensive_options.action: Granby roll to guard—invert toward the choking arm and roll through to establish closed or half guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When opponent has committed to the finish and arm extraction has failed. This is a late-stage emergency escape that requires flexibility and timing.
defensive_options.if_successful: Established in closed guard with the Darce grip broken or significantly weakened by the position change
defensive_options.risk: A failed granby can accelerate the choke if opponent maintains grip through the roll and ends up in a stronger finishing position

defensive_options.action: Frame and circle away—post your free hand on opponent's hip and walk your body away to reduce compression angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the choke is not yet deep and opponent's grip has gaps. Works best early before the figure-four is fully locked.
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates enough space to begin arm extraction or forces opponent to reset their grip, buying time
defensive_options.risk: Circling away without arm extraction only delays the finish; if you run out of mat space, you will be cornered

escape_paths: Arm extraction to turtle recovery—free the trapped arm and re-establish turtle or seated guard
Granby roll to closed guard—invert through the choke to break the grip angle and pull opponent into your guard
Step over to scramble—clear your leg over opponent's head to create a reversal or guard recovery opportunity

favorable_outcomes.how: Execute a granby roll toward the choking arm, inverting through the position. As you roll, the grip angle changes dramatically and often breaks the figure-four. Pull opponent into your closed guard as you complete the inversion and immediately control their posture to prevent re-establishing the grip.

Extract the trapped arm before the hip drop by gripping your own wrist with your free hand and pulling while turning your body into the attacker. Once the arm clears the choke structure, immediately establish frames and recover to turtle. The outcome returns to Darce Control position but with the choke structure broken, giving you a second chance to fully escape.

common_errors.error: Pulling head and body away from the choke in a panic response
common_errors.consequence: Moving away actually tightens the choke by elongating the neck in the direction of maximum compression, accelerating blood choke onset
common_errors.correction: Turn your body toward the attacker and tuck your chin tight. Moving into the choke reduces the angle needed for carotid compression and creates space on the exit side for arm extraction.

common_errors.error: Ignoring the trapped arm and focusing only on neck defense
common_errors.consequence: The trapped arm is the structural element that makes the Darce effective. Chin tucks and neck flexion can delay but not prevent the finish if the arm remains trapped.
common_errors.correction: Prioritize arm extraction using your free hand immediately. Pull the trapped arm toward your centerline while turning into the attacker. Removing the arm collapses the choke mechanics entirely.

common_errors.error: Allowing yourself to be flattened completely to the mat
common_errors.consequence: Flat on the mat eliminates all frame and hip escape leverage, making the attacker's hip drop and body extension maximally effective with no counter-leverage available
common_errors.correction: Maintain some base on your knees or hip. Post your free hand on the mat or against opponent's hip. If partially flattened, immediately work to get a knee under you to restore some elevation and framing ability.

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to tap when the choke is fully locked
common_errors.consequence: Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in 4-6 seconds once fully applied. Waiting to see if you can still escape after the hip drop and extension risks involuntary loss of consciousness.
common_errors.correction: If the hip drop is complete, body extension has begun, and you have no frame or arm extraction in progress, tap immediately. A submitted round is recoverable; brain hypoxia is not.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that your opponent is initiating the Darce Choke finish from Darce Control?
flashcards.answer: The key recognition cues are: opponent begins walking their hips toward the choking-arm side (moving from parallel to perpendicular), grip pressure increases noticeably as they pinch their elbows together, shoulder pressure intensifies as they drive weight forward into the side of your head, and their hip begins dropping toward the mat. The hip walk is usually the first detectable signal and provides the widest escape window—once the hip drops, your options narrow dramatically.

trap: Wait for the squeeze to react

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the Darce Choke to ensure safety in training?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel bilateral carotid compression with no active escape in progress. Specifically, if the attacker has completed the hip drop, locked the figure-four, and begun body extension while your arm remains trapped and you have no frame established, tap without hesitation. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in 4-6 seconds from full lock. In training, tap early and tap often—there is no training benefit to losing consciousness, and the positional learning comes from the escape attempts, not from enduring the finish.
flashcards.answer_line: Tap at full lock with no frame

plausible: Tap as arms wrap the neck
Escape first, tap only if stuck

flashcards.question: What is the highest-percentage defensive response when you feel the Darce grip tightening?
flashcards.answer: Arm extraction is the highest-percentage defense because it removes the structural element that makes the Darce choke functional. Use your free hand to grip your trapped arm at the wrist or forearm and pull it toward your centerline while simultaneously turning your body into the attacker. The turn reduces compression angle while the pull works to slide the arm out of the choke loop. This must be initiated before the hip drop—once the attacker's hip hits the mat, the compression makes arm extraction extremely difficult.

plausible: Bridge and try to sit up

flashcards.question: Why does moving away from the Darce Choke make it tighter, and what should you do instead?
flashcards.answer: Moving away elongates your neck in the direction of maximum compression—the choking arm acts as an anchor while your body movement stretches the carotid arteries against the forearm blade. Instead, turn your body toward the attacker, which shortens the distance between your shoulder and head, reducing the space available for the forearm to compress. Simultaneously tuck your chin to block deeper forearm penetration. Moving into the choke feels counterintuitive but is biomechanically correct for reducing compression and creating extraction angles.

plausible: Stay flat and wait it out

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the finishing sequence cues and building automatic defensive response
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes Darce Control and slowly initiates the finishing sequence. Defender calls out each cue as it occurs (hip walk, grip tighten, shoulder drop, hip drop). Build the habit of recognizing the sequence in order. No escape attempts yet—purely recognition and awareness training.

training_progressions.focus: Drilling each escape path against cooperative resistance
training_progressions.description: Practice arm extraction, step-over, and granby roll individually against 30% resistance. Partner holds the position and allows escape attempts, providing feedback on timing and mechanics. 10 reps each escape per side, focusing on correct body movement direction and arm extraction technique.

training_progressions.focus: Executing escapes under progressive resistance with time pressure
training_progressions.description: Partner applies the Darce finish at 50-75% intensity. Defender must escape or tap within 10 seconds. Track escape rate and identify which finishing variations cause the most difficulty. Increase resistance as escape rate improves above 40%. Emphasize tapping early when caught clean.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defense starting from established Darce Control
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring where attacker starts in locked Darce Control and works to finish while defender works to escape. Full resistance with safety emphasis. 2-minute rounds, reset after each finish or escape. Goal is recognizing defensive windows in real time and selecting the appropriate escape path based on attacker's positioning.
